analysis.one_liner: Bans new road building and logging in protected roadless areas of America's national forests.
analysis.headline: The Roadless Area Conservation Act won the backing of 95 House Democrats but never received a committee vote or floor vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write into law the existing 'Roadless Rule,' a 2001 regulation that bars the Forest Service from allowing road construction, road rebuilding, or logging in about 58 million acres of unroaded national forest land. Its sponsors argued that roadless forests supply drinking water to tens of millions of Americans, filter water so downstream communities save millions in treatment costs, and support hunting, fishing, and recreation jobs. Writing the rule into statute would make it much harder for a future administration to simply repeal it and open those areas to logging and road building.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who drink water that comes from national forest watersheds, hikers, hunters, anglers, campers, and the small-town recreation economies around roadless forests. The bill's findings say roadless areas provide drinking water to tens of millions of Americans and save downstream communities millions of dollars in water filtration costs, and that recreation-based economies depend on roadless public land for jobs and revenue [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Water drinkers, outdoor recreationists, and gateway towns

how_it_helps.text: Bars the Agriculture Department from allowing road construction, road reconstruction, or logging in inventoried roadless areas where the Roadless Rule already prohibits those activities, turning a regulation into permanent law [S2][S3].
Protects watersheds that the bill says supply drinking water to tens of millions of citizens and save downstream communities millions of dollars in water filtration costs [S3].
Preserves hunting, fishing, hiking, and other recreation the bill's findings call unparalleled opportunities, and supports recreation-based local economies that depend on unroaded public land [S3].

The bill does not impose new limits on access to private, state, or other federal land outside roadless areas, and leaves many existing uses, including mechanized travel and hydropower development, in place [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The timber industry, which would lose the ability to log in roadless areas, and road-building contractors who bid on Forest Service projects. The bill's sponsors argue this cost is small because the Forest Service already carries a $3.2 billion maintenance backlog on its 371,581-mile existing road system and because wildfires are almost twice as likely to start in roaded areas [S3].

drawbacks.text: Opponents of roadless protections have long argued that locking areas off from timber harvest and road access limits active forest management — the thinning, fuel reduction, and access needed to fight insects, disease, and severe wildfire. The bill's own text responds that wildfires are almost twice as likely in roaded areas and that fuel-reduction work continues to be prioritized, but that tradeoff is the core disagreement [S3].

The bill narrows the Forest Service's flexibility to adjust management of roadless areas case by case through planning, since the secretary would be barred from allowing road construction or logging wherever the Roadless Rule prohibits it [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefits — protected drinking water sources, wildlife habitat, and recreation on tens of millions of acres — are broad and permanent, while the costs fall on a single industry, commercial logging in roadless areas, which the Roadless Rule has already restricted since 2001. The main honest objection is that reduced timber and road access can constrain some forest management tools, and that question is genuinely debated among forest scientists. On balance the bill's costs are concentrated and modest; its benefits are diffuse and large.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in January 2021, split between two House committees, sent to subcommittees, got a single subcommittee hearing in May 2022, and then sat until the 117th Congress ended in January 2023 without ever reaching a committee or floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Ruben Gallego introduced the bill on January 12, 2021, with 64 original cosponsors listed in the introduction [S1][S3].
It was referred to both the Agriculture Committee and the Natural Resources Committee, a dual referral that requires two committees to act [S5].
In February 2021 it was sent to the Natural Resources Subcommittee on National Parks, Forests, and Public Lands and the Agriculture Subcommittee on Conservation and Forestry [S5].
The only recorded action after that was a subcommittee hearing on May 11, 2022; neither full committee ever held a markup or vote [S5].
The bill gathered 94 cosponsors, all Democrats, and died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S4][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Timber and road-building interests are better off because the bill died: they kept the legal status quo, where roadless protections rest on a regulation that a future administration can revise or repeal rather than on statute. No member or committee had to cast a recorded vote on it.

sides.party_line_note: All 94 cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican signed on; no vote was ever taken, so no roll-call record exists, but the sponsorship was entirely one-sided.

industries.note: The bill would permanently bar logging in inventoried roadless areas where the Roadless Rule already prohibits it, removing a supply of federal timber and ending the possibility that a future administration reopens those areas. The industry's access to those trees comes at the cost of the public watershed and recreation values the bill protects.

Road builders would lose potential Forest Service contracts for new roads into roadless areas. The bill's findings note the Forest Service already has a $3.2 billion maintenance backlog on existing roads, so maintenance work would continue.

The bill's findings say recreation-based economies depend on unroaded public land for jobs, revenue, and consumer spending, and that roadless areas support hunting, fishing, and backcountry recreation that ordinary visitors use.

industries.industry: Water utilities and downstream water users
industries.note: Undisturbed forest watersheds filter water naturally; the bill's findings say keeping roadless areas roadless saves downstream communities millions of dollars in water filtration costs and protects drinking water for tens of millions of people.
